1784.d:
WORLDS APART brings to life a dead hacked script once destined for the Ethereum blockchain and brings it over to the world of Tezos, glitch-induced randomness and all. 

"HUH? What are you talking about...." 

ETH tx hashes are all hexadecimal, Tezos hashes are not. The original script relied on parsing hex numbers from the hash to perform a set of instructions to generate the artwork. Because Tezos hashes are not hexadecimal, though occasionally contain characters from the hex charset, the hex processing mechanism was left in place. This resulted in occasional failures of individual instructions within the instruction set, inducing a sort of beautiful randomness. Far less dots and curves are rendered than the original script as a result of most characters being non-hex, delivering a cleaner aesthetic and a more meaningful representation. 

No spoilers on traits, except that SOME EDITIONS WILL BE SIGNED ;)

Thank you for minting <3

1795.d:
Of all the artworks I have made, this highly conceptual work is my favorite.

This NFT simulates natural selection in a limited population. 

Each individual in the population has their own DNA: a string of 41 letters. In the first generation of the simulation, each individual has completely random DNA.

For each new generation, the two 'fittest' individuals from the previous generation are allowed to reproduce, with their offspring carrying a combination of the DNA of both parents and some random mutations. 

The fitness of an individual is given by the number of letters of their DNA that match the sentence: "Natural selection is anything but random" (a quote from Richard Dawkins).

In total, 40 generations are simulated. The DNA of the fittest individual from each odd-numbered generation is printed.

The probability of a random piece of DNA equals the quote is one in 95^41 ≈ 10^80, roughly the number of atoms in the universe.

Source code: https://turtletoy.net/turtle/2f92cd6aa3

An interactive tiled pattern is generated with the fxhash which determines two features at random.

"groundsState" value determines a base configuration and is sampled uniformly at random in the range 0 to 1.

"spectralGap" determines the color of the pattern and comes in three types::
'low' (30%) is monochrome
'mid' (60%) is small hue range
'high' (10%) is a large hue range

*click/touch & hold/move* the canvas to charge the pattern and change the flux mode of the tiles.
*release* the canvas and the pattern decays back to its "groundState" value.

1882.d:
Some people describe creative coding as 'Computer Magick' and I agree, there is some degree of mysticism involved. Taking a physical phenomena and distorting it so that is no longer real is what Imaginary Resonances is about.

There is a surface and sand is dropped on it. The surface vibrates and ushers the sand into patterns. What kind of sound could have made the surface vibrate like that?

The algorithm behind Imaginary Resonances is simple variation on Chladni figures: figures that arise when sand is dropped on a vibrating surface.

Made by Sam Tsao (@sam___tsao) with p5

1897.d:
A slowly-changing landscape of multi-hued layers, shifting and evolving over time.

The number of stripes is generated from the hash value, with values ranging between six and twelve: higher and lower values are rarer.

The stability affects how rapidly the colours and orientation of the stripes change. The effects are subtle, but there is a significant difference between a hash value which tends towards 'Steady' and one which produces 'Erratic'. Again, extremes are rarer.

Obliquity refers to the variation in parallel stripes with three possible values. The middle value, with a gentle tilt, is most prevalent.

Stacking and rotation are both linked. The image is generated either horizontally or vertically, and the stripes are stacked from one edge. All possibilities are equally likely.

Palette style varies from a vivid, saturated palette, down to the rare-but-beautiful monochrome mode.

1904.d:
Forgotten Souls is ZingRex's first generative project on fxhash. 

In my mind, no one ever truly leaves us. Everyone is and remains a permanent part of this universe. You may visualise them in a pattern while going for a stroll in a park, see them as unusual constellations in the night sky, as tiled artwork on mosaic, or even as rivulets of colour that pops every time you close your eyes. Forgotten Souls has been built with pixel art to capture those fleeting glimpses.

The colours have not been contrasted intentionally and left to randomisation, just the way patterns are seen in nature - it is only in the eyes of the beholder. Some patterns may feel calm and serene, while others fiery; some passionate, while others nightmarish. The Soul Detail can be of 3 types - Flat Tiles, Intricate Carvings and Micro Dots (Micro Dots being the most rare).

Why 333 ? I would love this to be part 1 of a two-part series which will take the total number to 666.

Forgotten Souls. A Genesis collection. Created on p5

Isn't it beautiful to know that everything is constantly changing? From our bodies, to the objects around us, nature, planets and everything else in our universe.

The only thing that keeps us from accepting this constant state of flux is our own minds. It likes certainty, it fears change, it wants everything to stay as it is.

This art piece is a representation of that constant imperfect state of change. From calm and focused movements to more erratic, aggressive versions of the same piece.

Written in glsl to leverage the power of the gpu, projected onto an orthographic quad.

1917.d:
Crypt-o-show is a parody art gallery generator, inspired by a very disappointing and comical NFT show produced by Christies. The infamous show displayed Artblock works on unsuitable screens, installed closely together, over a large squiggle on the wall. The generator creates a little gallery with a random selection of artworks that parody AB pieces – these are used as features in this work – forming a mini collection of collectibles. 

Crypt-o-show is a form of ‘institutional critique’ through generative art, and about generative art, poking fun at the both the market for on-chain generative artwork collections made addictive through their lottery mechanics, as well as mocking the traditional auction house and its blundering and inelegant support for these new digital practices. 

"The saddest thing you'll see today is, once again, brought to you by Christie's."
- @MPtherealmvp (twitter.com/MPtherealmvp/status/1442917552871526401)

1919.d:
PixlFlippr is an offshoot of my "Simple Harmonic Motion" series, inspired by the complexity of life emerging through the interaction of simple 'dumb' behaviors, with intricate details emerging on multiple scales. PixlFlippr operates on a pixel level (in the form of a GLSL frag shader).

Every pixel oscillates at a single fixed frequency, slightly out-of-sync with its neighbors. There is no explicit pixel-neighborhood communication (as there would be in eg Cellular Automata), and every pixel acts autonomously, oblivious to its surroundings. Yet collectively, the entire system exhibits constantly evolving complex high level behavior on many scales, ranging from patterns & behaviors spanning a few pixels, all the way up to the level of the entire image. These are further amplified through the emergent pixel aliasing artefacts & moiré patterns. 

Also, it's trippy af. 

PS All generative mints are a seamless loop with a loop duration ranging from a few minutes to over an hour. So stick around & watch it mutate!

1920.d:
In art, and in generative art especially, we often find ourselves with loose ends, experiments that don't make the final piece. These go often unappreciated and are left unpublished and unseen. When making my last project Mycenae I (re)discovered a number of related attractors. Rhea has sharp corners in place of sweeping arcs. Phoebe turns back on itself, long curves join at harsh vertices. 

Both strange attractors are fractals, containing infinite detail. The token contains the generation parameters and so represents the fractal at a deeper level than the image itself. 

I included my debug renderer as an Easter egg. You would be lucky to find it.

The naming comes from a convention I have picked up from habit. Coding projects are named for Greek figures of myth. Generative tokens should be named for ancient centres of Greek civilisation. The attractors I named for titans and, since they are all related, Saturnian moons.

1924.d:
An interactive chaotic attractor based on a circular harmonograph.

This piece rewards patience.  After the initial structure forms, watch the attractor develop as more iterations are added and the details resolve.  The image will continue to refine itself forever; there is no limit on the iteration number.  Pause, unpause, generate and export jpgs at very high resolutons (see controls below).

This is a generalisation of a piece donated to the Edible East science and art trail on our global sustainable food future, and 100% of every sale and secondary royal1ties will be donated to local food banks.

Controls:  

To stop/restart the attractor iterating, press SPACE.
To switch to a high resolution canvas, press 1-9.  The canvas width will become n*1000 by n*1000 (so 2000x2000 if you press '2') and the attractor will restart.
To export the current canvas as a jpeg, press X.
To update the whole image with current data, press U (helpful if using a high resolution).
To invert, press I.

No-input Mixer draws a canvas starting with an empty window, goes in to a feedback loop, then continues looping through alternating displacements.

Colors are divided into:

- Monochrome (50%)
- Red/Cyan (20%)
- Yellow/Blue (20%)
- Magenta/Green (10%)

Possibility of inverted output (30%)

Displacements are affected by hash. Other features include pixelation size, direction, separation and the amount of noisy area. 

"I think I find an equal relationship with no-input mixing board, which I didn't see with the guitar. When I played the guitar, "I" had to play the guitar. But with the mixing board, the machine would play me and the music would play the other two, and I would do something or maybe nothing."
- Toshimaru Nakamura
